WHAT THE SLOT IS FOR: slot 14 named the maintenance level as a percentage; this converts it into a PRICE, and adds the three other ways an outside party acts on your position under a published rule. The observation that makes the price computable is that the loan does not shrink when the position falls -- only equity absorbs it -- so the threshold arrives sooner than the percentage suggests, and the call price contains neither your entry nor your stop. NUMBERS, every cell re-run in Python and cross-checked so that equity at the call value equals the requirement exactly: $20,000 position, $10,000 own, loan $10,000, 30% requirement gives a call at $14,286 and a 28.6% fall. The grid runs 100% equity (never) down to 33.3% (4.8% at a 30% requirement, and already breached at 35%). SECOND READ FOUND: '7.1% is an ordinary fortnight in an ordinary stock', an unmeasured frequency claim of exactly the class the slot 10, 11 and 13 reads each caught, now tied to slot 12's measured mid-cap range (2.84 average days, so 'under three'); 'you can know all of it by Thursday', a flourish that contradicted the claim's own 'takes an evening'; 'describing a Tuesday', which is slot 14's idiom and would have been the second use in adjacent lessons; a cross-reference to lesson 12 for a point about position size, which is slot 20's subject and not slot 12's; and a corporate-actions paragraph that was a FIFTH item under a claim naming four, cut rather than widening the claim. The budget gate refused the lesson three times at 1,898, 1,810 and 1,802 words before it came in at 1,800. EXPANDED AFTER THE WORD CEILING WAS REMOVED. This is the one lesson the 1,800-word gate demonstrably bound: it was refused at 1,898, 1,810 and 1,802 before landing at exactly 1,800, which is trimming to satisfy a number rather than because anything repeated itself. Re-read against the donor (old lesson 13, recovered from git at d2f23868c) under the new standard, the question being 'what did a student need that I left out?', and SIX things had been lost. (1) The stop-versus-call distinction, which is the most useful sentence in the donor's Part 1: a stop is an instruction to the market and a maintenance call is an instruction to the account holder, so in a gap the two arrive together and the stop is the slower, because it can only act on trades that print and the broker need not wait for those. (2) Regulation T and FINRA Rule 4210 were never named in the body, nor were the 25% floor and the 30%+ house requirement, so a reader had nothing to look up; restored WITHOUT restating slot 14, which already teaches that there are two requirements set by different people. (3) The single most common error in the subject -- reading the requirement as the fall -- was not warned against anywhere, and the donor's quiz distractor analysis was the only place it appeared. (4) The concrete covered-call consequence: premium kept, shares gone at the strike, dividend collected by someone else. (5) Pin risk was described but never NAMED, so a reader meeting the term elsewhere could not connect it. (6) The limit up-limit down band DOUBLES in the last twenty-five minutes, which is exactly when a stop is most likely to be reached. And (7) corporate actions, cut originally for being a fifth item under a claim naming four -- the claim now says five, which is the honest fix, and the section covers splits, reverse splits, special dividends and spin-offs moving the printed price and tripping every level-based order at once. 1,800 to 2,398 words. TRANSLATION: only 19 strings were new, so the other 115 kept their existing translations. Two hazards were caught before writing. The shared memory key 'you' is nominative in every locale (de 'du', ru 'вы', and tr 'siz' and pt 'você', which are also the WRONG register for this corpus), and it cannot be changed without rewriting every other lesson that uses it -- so the you split was removed and the emphasis carried by the sentence instead. And Pin risk opened its sentence, which meant the fragment after it began with a preserved space that lands mid-sentence in Japanese between the katakana term and its particle; the English was restructured so the term sits inside the sentence and the fragment after it opens on a comma. CHECKERS THEN FOUND Spanish inventing a '50' where the English says 'half', and five strings identical to English -- 'pin risk' in es/fr/it/pt, which is genuine market usage there and matches the article-carrying forms already in memory, and 'Corporate actions' in nl; all registered. THE READ THEN FOUND what no checker could: Arabic had 'هذا هو' (masculine singular) against 'مخاطر' (feminine plural), recast to name the state so the agreement holds and the following clause has an explicit subject; and German read 'ist Pin-Risiko' where 'heißt' is the verb that names a term.

SOURCE: old lesson 12, 3,773 words, and the worst offender left in the beginner tier: a composite trader ('Mark Sullivan, 27, software engineer', labelled a composite in the text) with an eight-week week-by-week collapse, an invented $6,080 loss, a $4,800 opportunity cost, a recovery arc, a case-study quiz about him and three comparison panels restating his numbers. Five emoji headings, five callouts, a 'Signal Pilot Integration' block. The whole narrative is gone: it is precisely what 'one worked example, not a story' exists to remove, and it is the same defect task 20 stripped from 32 other lessons. WHAT THE SLOT IS FOR, and it is the right close for the module: a simulator sets to zero every number Module 2 spent six lessons measuring, so the module has already given the reader everything needed to undo the flattery. The syllabus splits the failure in two -- cost and consequence -- and the lesson prices the first EXACTLY and deliberately refuses to put a number on the second, which is the honest position for a lesson whose whole subject is the difference between a measured cost and an assumed one. NUMBERS, all re-run in Python: slot 12's mid-cap, $10,000 as 250 shares, 1% stop so $100 at risk. One full spread $12.50 + $2.00 commission + $2.50 slippage = $17.00 a round trip, so slot 10's s = 0.17 and the breakeven win rate moves from 50.0% to 58.5%. A hundred trades at a 55% win rate therefore reports +$1,000 in the simulator and nets MINUS $700 -- the strategy never worked, and 55% was below breakeven the whole time. The same $10,000 gives 51.2% on slot 12's top row and 251% on its bottom row. SECOND READ FOUND: an empty table header leaving the row labels unlabelled; 'finds the whole of the underperformance in the gap', which overstates Barber and Odean; and two comparison claims gestured at rather than given, now printed as 51.2% and 251% and both verified. RE-READ UNDER THE NEW STANDARD (word ceiling removed). Against the donor (recovered at 74c0086c6) the deletions were overwhelmingly correct -- the Mark Sullivan composite, its week-by-week collapse, the case-study quiz about him, three comparison panels restating his numbers and a five-gap table are all invented performance data and stay deleted. But TWO substantive things had gone out with him. (1) The donor listed rejection risk -- limit orders that do not fill -- among the things a simulator cannot teach, and the rebuild covered only the market-order gift. The limit-order version is the subtler and more expensive one: a simulator fills your limit the moment price touches it, while live a touch is not a fill because slot 3's queue is in front of you, so a simulator silently inflates any strategy built on resting orders because such a strategy never misses in it. (2) The donor's one piece of non-narrative advice, paper to micro to live and never skip the middle. The rebuild established that a simulator cannot teach consequence and then left the reader with no answer to 'so what does?'. The argument survives the deletion of the composite entirely: fear at a few dollars a trade teaches exactly what fear at several hundred teaches, and the difference is only that one of them leaves an account to apply the lesson to; stepping from a simulator straight to full size makes the first experience of real money and the first experience of real size arrive on the same trade. 1,652 to 1,954 words, four new strings, eleven locales clean.

SOURCE: old lesson 9, 2,915 words, which the syllabus names as the donor for BOTH this slot and slot 20 -- its Part 1 is expectancy and its Parts 2 to 5 are sizing. Only Part 1 came here. The two setups and their R figures are the donor's own and were re-derived rather than copied: 70% winning at a quarter the loser is 0.70 x 0.25 - 0.30 = -0.125R, 40% winning at five times is 0.40 x 5 - 0.60 = +1.40R. FORWARD OBLIGATION, recorded here because it is easy to miss: slot 20's page still carries that Part 1 verbatim, so when slot 20 is rebuilt the expectancy half must be REMOVED, not rewritten, or the two lessons will teach the same thing twice; slot 20's prereq also still points at 'Lesson 08: Confirmation Bias', which no longer exists at 8. WHAT THE SLOT IS FOR: the donor states expectancy in dollars first and only then converts to R, which makes R look like a presentational convenience. Here it is the claim -- E is quoted in R because that is what makes it survive a change of account, instrument and position, so the number you computed last year is comparable with today's. The move the donor never makes is the one that ties the module together: set E to zero and solve, and breakeven p = (1 + s) / (b + 1), which is slot 10's s from the previous module entering by simple subtraction. NUMBERS, all re-run: the table's no-cost column is 1/(b+1) and its right-hand column is 1.17/(b+1). Its middle row is the point of the whole lesson -- b = 1 gives 50.0% and 58.5%, which are exactly the figures slot 10 and slot 16 arrived at independently, so both of those were this formula with b fixed at 1 and neither said so. SECOND READ FOUND: 'the first loses money on every trade it takes', which the bounds section contradicts three paragraphs later by saying E is an average -- a setup winning 70% of the time plainly does not lose on every trade; now 'on average' in both places. A claim that slot 10 'left it' at 50%, when slot 10 printed 50.8% and 53.9%, both after costs -- 50% is the base it started FROM, and that is what it now says. 'The winners cut early, the losers held a little longer than the plan said', an unmeasured behavioural claim about the reader, the same defect the slot 10, 11, 13, 14 and 15 reads each caught once; replaced by the structural statement that the gap lives in the exits rather than the entries. And problem 3's 'b raised by half', which reads as either x1.5 or +0.5 -- now 'multiplied by 1.5', with 'five percentage points' made explicit alongside it for the same reason. TRANSLATION READS FOUND: the two words this lesson turns on collide with the house term for expectancy in three Romance locales -- es/pt 'esperanza'/'esperança' and it 'speranza' all mean BOTH 'expectancy' and 'hope', so the claim's 'you have a hope about one' would have read as 'you have an expectancy of one', which is the opposite of what the sentence says; es and pt use 'ilusión'/'ilusão' instead and it keeps 'speranza' only because its expectancy term is 'aspettativa' and does not collide. Japanese hit the same thing with 期待 inside 期待値 and uses 望み. German 'ein gut besuchter Weg' for 'a well-populated way' is comprehensible but not idiomatic (vielbegangen is), and the Kelly citation's 'der festhält' had no antecedent -- the nearest noun is a quoted English title -- so 'der Aufsatz, der festhält' names it; 'Sizing-Regel' was replaced by the German the corpus already uses. Найди' in adjacent problems and 'способ отказать' where 'давать сбой' is the idiom. Turkish stacked three colons in the prereq because 'Ön koşullar:' already ends on one, moved to the dash apposition the Arabic prereqs use -- which meant supplying the leading space the source does not have after -- and had 'son elli işlemin hakkındaki', where hakkında governs the bare noun. found: SOURCE: none of its own. The syllabus marks slot 19 NEW and gives old lesson 55 to slot 18, but old 55's Part 3 is this slot's subject, so 55 was read end to end before either was written -- which is why 19 is being written BEFORE 18: whatever 18 keeps, 19 has first claim on the detection arithmetic, and building 18 first would have shipped a Next button and a closing paragraph that had to be re-translated across eleven locales to repair. What old 55 also carried and is NOT coming here: a composite trader ('Devin Osei', four years of records, 380 logged trades, an 11R drawdown) with a two-paragraph post-mortem, a 'Where Signal Pilot Fits' section that opens by conceding no indicator answers this question, a three-question quiz restating Parts 1 to 3, a six-bullet takeaways box restating them again, and a five-part practice exercise. 3,758 words down to 1,621. WHAT THE SLOT IS FOR: slot 17 closed by saying E computed from a handful of trades is not an E and that the sample needed is larger than anyone expects. This puts the number on it. The spine is that sigma comes out of the SAME two inputs as E -- sigma^2 = p*b^2 + (1-p) - E^2 -- so the noise is not an extra assumption, it is already in the numbers the reader has. NUMBERS, all re-run and every one reproducible from the constants the lesson prints: p = 0.45 at b = 2 gives E = +0.35R, variance 2.2275, sigma = 1.4925R, so sigma/E = 4.26 on a single trade. The 95% interval on the measured E is +/-1.96*sigma/sqrt(n): at the FIFTY trades slot 17's own problem 1 asks for it runs -0.06R to +0.76R and contains zero, and its half-width (0.414R) is larger than the expectancy it surrounds, which is what the claim asserts literally rather than loosely. At 200 it is +0.14R to +0.56R, top nearly four times the bottom (3.89). Sample sizes use n = K*sigma^2/delta^2 with K = (1.960 + 0.842)^2 = 7.8512: 143 trades to separate the edge from zero, 571 to catch a halving, 2,284 to catch a quarter. THE RESULT THE SOURCE NEVER HAD, and the reason this lesson belongs after Module 2 rather than anywhere else: subtracting a constant from every trade moves the mean and leaves the variance untouched, so slot 10's s = 0.17 takes E from 0.35R to 0.18R, sigma/E from 4.26 to 8.29, and the 'is there an edge at all' sample from 143 trades to 540 -- a factor of 3.78. The charges do not just halve the edge; they nearly quadruple the evidence needed to prove there is one. AND THE ONE WORTH KEEPING: at n = 70 the significance threshold 1.96*sigma/sqrt(70) = 0.3496R lands on the true expectancy of 0.3500R, so the power there is 50% by construction -- seventy trades is an exact coin flip on whether a real edge shows up as significant. That is why the confidence-interval answer (70) and the power answer (143) differ, and stating both is what stops the two looking like a contradiction. SECOND READ FOUND: 'the threshold sits precisely on your true expectancy, so your odds are exactly even' -- 0.3496 is not 0.3500, and a reader checking it would find the overstatement, now 'almost exactly' and 'as near even as makes no difference'. 'The same record is equally compatible with an edge nearly four times larger' -- values inside a confidence interval are NOT equally supported, the likelihood peaks at the estimate; now 'consistent with'. The worked example gave E = +0.35R and in the same sentence checked it against lesson 17's 39.0%, which is the AFTER-costs breakeven, so 0.35R read as though it were net when the whole close of the lesson depends on it not being; now labelled 'before costs' with the costs explicitly deferred. The sources line said 7.85 'is (1.96 + 0.84)^2', which computes to 7.84 and gives 2,281 rather than the 2,284 in the table -- now quoted at the precision the table was built at. A three-clause sentence that did not parse ('a change of regime makes the trades ... samples from two different systems'). And two attention-directives in one lesson ('the sentence to sit with', 'read the middle row'), one of which is also slot 17's device two lessons earlier; the first was cut.
